## Welcome

This is a starter Quarto document (`demo_r.qmd`) for writing reproducible data science reports in **R**.

To render or preview this document:

* Click the **Render** / **Preview** button at the top right of the editor in VS Code, Positron, or RStudio (shortcut: `Ctrl+Shift+K` or `Cmd+Shift+K`), or
* Run `quarto render demo_r.qmd` in the terminal.

## 1. Load Packages

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
```

## 2. Read and Inspect Data

Let's load the parkrun dataset included in `00_data/ParkRunPerformanceData.xlsx` and inspect the first few rows:

```{r}
parkrun <- read_excel(
  "00_data/ParkRunPerformanceData.xlsx",
  sheet = "Sheet1",
  col_types = c("date", "numeric")
)
names(parkrun) <- c("date", "runtime")

glimpse(parkrun)
summary(parkrun)
```

## 3. Visualise the Data

We can plot runtimes over time with a trend line using `ggplot2`:

```{r}
#| label: fig-runtime-trend
#| fig-cap: "Parkrun runtimes over time with a smoothed trend line."
ggplot(parkrun, aes(x = date, y = runtime)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, colour = "#1f77b4") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#d62728") +
  labs(
    title = "Parkrun Runtimes Over Time",
    x = "Event Date",
    y = "Run Time (minutes)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 4. Download and Visualise Train Data

The [Office of Rail and Road (ORR) Data API](https://api.dataportal.orr.gov.uk/) publishes train performance data as machine-readable tables. No API key is needed. Below we download [table 3114a](https://dataportal.orr.gov.uk/statistics/performance/passenger-rail-performance/table-3114a-public-performance-measure-by-operator-and-sector/), which gives the percentage of trains arriving at their destination on time in each four-week railway period, and reshape it so that there is one row per period and operator:

```{r}
#| label: train-download
#| message: false

library(jsonlite)

train_url <- "https://api.dataportal.orr.gov.uk/api/tables/performance/3114a"
train_raw <- fromJSON(train_url)

train <- train_raw |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -time_period,
    names_to = "operator",
    values_to = "on_time_pct"
  ) |>
  transmute(
    # Period labels look like "Apr 2019 to Mar 2020 (Period 01)"
    date = parse_date(
      paste("01", str_extract(time_period, "^[A-Za-z]{3} \\d{4}")),
      format = "%d %b %Y"
    ),
    operator = str_remove(operator, "^(national|sector|franchised|open_access)_"),
    # ORR uses "[z]" where data do not apply; parse_number() converts those to NA
    on_time_pct = suppressWarnings(parse_number(on_time_pct))
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(on_time_pct))

glimpse(train)
```

We can now plot the national trend alongside two operators. Because the data are downloaded when the document is rendered, the plot updates automatically when ORR publishes new periods:

```{r}
#| label: fig-train-punctuality
#| fig-cap: "Share of trains arriving on time in each four-week period. Source: ORR Data API, table 3114a."

operators_to_plot <- c(
  "great_britain",
  "london_and_south_east",
  "london_north_eastern_railway"
)

train |>
  filter(operator %in% operators_to_plot) |>
  mutate(operator = str_to_title(str_replace_all(operator, "_", " "))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = date, y = on_time_pct, colour = operator)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of trains arriving on time",
    subtitle = "Great Britain, London & South East services and LNER",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Trains arriving on time",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Office of Rail and Road, table 3114a (via ORR Data API)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Bus stops in Leeds

```{r}
library(osmextract)
bus_stops <- oe_get("Leeds, UK", layer = "points")
names(bus_stops)
```
